interactions.label: What anatomical feature explains why femoral hernias have the highest strangulat

params.question: What anatomical feature explains why femoral hernias have the highest strangulation risk among groin hernias?

answers.text: They pass through the deep inguinal ring, which is muscular and contractile

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The deep inguinal ring is the entry point for indirect inguinal hernias, not femoral hernias. Its muscular surround can stretch, actually lowering strangulation risk.

answers.text: They traverse a canal whose neck is formed by narrow, rigid ligamentous boundaries

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The femoral canal is bounded by rigid ligaments that cannot stretch, so even slight swelling of the contents rapidly compromises blood supply.

answers.text: They bulge through Hesselbach's triangle, a poorly supported area of the posterior wall

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hesselbach's triangle is the site of direct inguinal hernias. Its relatively wide defect actually gives direct hernias the lowest strangulation risk.

answers.text: They arise from a congenital patent processus vaginalis that narrows with age

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A patent processus vaginalis underlies indirect inguinal hernias, not femoral hernias. Femoral hernias are acquired defects unrelated to embryological remnants.

overallFeedback.feedback: Femoral hernias pass through the femoral canal, whose neck is bounded by rigid ligaments. This narrow, unyielding ring means even a small amount of swelling can strangulate the contents.
The femoral canal's rigid, unyielding neck is the reason femoral hernias strangulate more often than any other groin hernia — always repair them promptly.

params.question: A 70-year-old woman presents with a tender, irreducible lump below the right groin crease and vomiting since morning. Her abdomen is distending. What is the most appropriate management?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Watchful waiting applies only to minimally symptomatic, reducible inguinal hernias. This patient has signs of strangulation and obstruction — delay risks bowel necrosis.
Elective repair is appropriate for uncomplicated reducible hernias. A tender, irreducible lump with vomiting and distension indicates strangulation — a surgical emergency.

answers.text: Urgent surgery with assessment of bowel viability

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This presentation — irreducible, tender femoral hernia with intestinal obstruction — indicates strangulation. Immediate surgery is needed to relieve constriction, assess viability, and resect any non-viable bowel.
Resuscitation measures including NG decompression are part of initial management, but antibiotics alone cannot relieve mechanical strangulation. Definitive surgical relief is essential.

overallFeedback.feedback: This patient has a strangulated femoral hernia causing intestinal obstruction. She needs immediate surgery — there is no time for watchful waiting or elective scheduling.
A strangulated hernia is a surgical emergency. Resuscitate, operate urgently, relieve the constriction, and resect any non-viable bowel.

interactions.label: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in a patient with cirrhotic ascites requires u

params.question: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in a patient with cirrhotic ascites requires urgent surgical intervention.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: SBP is primary peritonitis — there is no perforation or leakage to repair. It is monomicrobial, occurring in cirrhotic ascites, and is treated with antibiotics alone. Surgery is not required and would be harmful.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — SBP is primary peritonitis with no surgically correctable source. It is monomicrobial and treated with antibiotics alone. Surgery would cause harm, not benefit.

params.question: A patient with board-like abdominal rigidity has an erect chest X-ray showing free gas under the diaphragm. Which of the following correctly describes the significance of this finding and the required management?

answers.text: It confirms intestinal obstruction; manage with nasogastric decompression and observation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Intestinal obstruction produces dilated loops and air-fluid levels, not free subdiaphragmatic gas. Free gas indicates perforation, which demands surgical source control.

answers.text: It confirms perforation of a hollow viscus; manage with resuscitation, antibiotics, and surgical source control

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Free gas beneath the diaphragm confirms pneumoperitoneum from a perforated hollow organ. All three pillars apply simultaneously: resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and urgent surgical source control.

answers.text: It confirms spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; manage with antibiotics alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: SBP occurs in cirrhotic ascites without perforation — there is no free gas on imaging. Free subdiaphragmatic gas points to secondary peritonitis requiring surgical source control.

answers.text: It is inconclusive; a CT scan is needed before any intervention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Free gas under the diaphragm on erect CXR is never inconclusive — it confirms perforation. While CT may help localise the source, the finding already indicates the need for urgent surgical intervention.

overallFeedback.feedback: Free gas beneath the diaphragm on erect CXR confirms a perforated hollow viscus. This is secondary peritonitis requiring all three pillars simultaneously: resuscitation, IV antibiotics, and urgent surgical source control.
Free subdiaphragmatic gas confirms perforation. The three pillars — resuscitation, antibiotics, and source control — must run in parallel, not one after the other.

params.question: A patient develops a swinging fever and localised pelvic pain two weeks after appendicectomy. Contrast-enhanced CT confirms a pelvic abscess. What is the most appropriate first-line management?

answers.text: Broad-spectrum antibiotics alone and reassessment in one week

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Antibiotics cannot penetrate the abscess wall. A walled-off collection will persist unless it is drained — antibiotics are adjunctive, not definitive.
Correct. Percutaneous drainage under CT or ultrasound guidance is first-line for an accessible intra-abdominal abscess. It evacuates pus that antibiotics alone cannot reach.
Surgical drainage is reserved for collections that fail percutaneous drainage or are inaccessible. For a pelvic abscess visible on CT, image-guided drainage is tried first.

answers.text: Wide en bloc excision of the collection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: En bloc excision is the management principle for retroperitoneal sarcomas, not for abscesses. An abscess is drained, not resected.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle: pus must be drained. Image-guided percutaneous drainage under CT or ultrasound is first-line for intra-abdominal abscesses. Surgical drainage is the fallback when percutaneous access fails.
An intra-abdominal abscess must be drained — antibiotics alone cannot clear walled-off pus. Image-guided percutaneous drainage is the first-line approach.
